claims.text: The as-deposited FeMnNiGeSi-type melt-spun microribbons have an ordered single-phase hexagonal structure.
The baseline microribbons undergo a sharp, hysteretic first-order magnetostructural transition.
The controlled intervention is approximately 10% cold rolling at room temperature followed by annealing at 300°C for 30 minutes in Ar.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment induces an optimal dislocation network in the microribbons.
The tailored dislocations act as distributed heterogeneous nucleation sites for the magnetostructural transformation.
Increasing the controlled dislocation density lowers the nucleation activation-energy barrier for the first-order magnetostructural transition.
Distributed nucleation sites cause more gradual nucleation and growth of the transformed phase.
The more gradual transformation broadens the temperature range of the magnetocaloric transition.
The more gradual transformation reduces hysteresis under low applied magnetic fields.
Treated microribbons will exhibit a broader entropy-change-versus-temperature profile than the untreated baseline.
Treated microribbons will exhibit significantly less hysteresis than the untreated baseline.
The treatment may slightly reduce the peak entropy change because the transformation is distributed over a wider temperature range.
The treatment is expected to improve magnetocaloric cycle stability.
The treatment is expected to improve heat exchange relative to the untreated microribbons.
The predictions apply within a processing window near 10% cold work and a 300°C anneal under low applied magnetic fields.
Excessive strain or higher annealing temperatures may generate uncontrolled defect states that compromise magnetic properties or mechanical stability.
Temperature-dependent magnetic measurements can indicate phase transformations and microstructural evolution in melt-spun materials.
TEM imaging or XRD line broadening can be used to quantify the treatment-induced dislocation density.
Failure to obtain both transition broadening and hysteresis reduction despite a confirmed increase in dislocation density would falsify the proposed mediation mechanism.
A drastic loss of entropy-change performance without improved cycling stability would count against the hypothesis.
